prosePairReviews.scienceReason: Q=I^2Rt is preserved as resistive heat energy, not transmitted power. With constant R and I defined as RMS over the heating interval, it agrees with R times the integral of instantaneous current squared. The steady-DC limit is stated correctly. Separation of generators and users explains transmission without an absolute storage prohibition.
prosePairReviews.equivalenceReason: Both versions identify Q as energy converted to heat, I as RMS current, t as elapsed conduction time, and steady DC as constant current. Both reject the same absolute inability-to-store inference without claiming unlimited or lossless storage.

prosePairReviews.scienceReason: The ordinary same-resistivity conductor comparison gives increasing resistance with length and decreasing resistance with cross-sectional area. The prose distinguishes material/cost tradeoffs from resistive heating and does not declare long-distance transmission inherently uneconomic or lower current the only possible intervention.
prosePairReviews.equivalenceReason: The same material/area comparison, dependence of economic consequences on transmitted power, increased material cost, and qualified importance of reducing current are retained in both languages.

prosePairReviews.scienceReason: For unchanged active power, power factor and circuit configuration, P=k U_rms I_rms PF implies inverse voltage/current scaling. Together with the preceding resistance model, lower RMS current reduces I-squared-R heating. No unity-power-factor assumption or comparison at fixed load impedance is substituted. The source's 500 kV and 16-20 kV values remain examples, not universal standards or generator ceilings.
prosePairReviews.equivalenceReason: Active power, power factor, configuration and RMS qualifiers are explicit in both versions. Both preserve the same voltage numbers and insulation/cost constraints and reject the same universal-limit interpretations.

prosePairReviews.scienceReason: The reciprocal current/voltage factor is confined to a lossless ideal transformer with matching power-factor and connection conventions. In the normal power-delivery direction, winding and core losses make real output active power less than input active power, so the ideal current relation is not an unconditional exact real-device result.
prosePairReviews.equivalenceReason: Both specify output relative to input, the same inverse scaling, ideal losslessness, equal power factors and corresponding connections. Both distinguish real active-power losses from the ideal case.

prosePairReviews.scienceReason: Receiving equipment requires voltage appropriate to its rating. Step-down transformation is correctly restricted to an AC supply and is not presented as direct transformation of steady DC.
prosePairReviews.equivalenceReason: The lathe-motor and lighting examples, rating-based voltage requirement, receiving-end location and AC step-down role have the same meaning in both versions.

prosePairReviews.scienceReason: The staged-distribution discussion uses the preceding fixed-power AC comparison, retaining its power-factor qualification. It explicitly separates that comparison from actual branch currents, which depend on individual loads; there is no claim that current necessarily rises in every downstream conductor.
prosePairReviews.equivalenceReason: Both describe staged voltage reduction and branching, keep the same-power/power-factor condition, reject the same downstream-current generalization, and refer to schematic figure 63 without asserting its pending visual correctness.

prosePairReviews.scienceReason: Corona is correctly described as a possible discharge in air near the conductor surface, tied to local electric field and conductor size/arrangement rather than a universal voltage threshold. AC peak voltage matters to that field. Appropriate design controls losses; the prose does not promise their complete elimination or locate corona exclusively across the entire inter-conductor gap.
prosePairReviews.equivalenceReason: Possible occurrence, near-surface location, field/geometry dependence, peak-voltage attention and loss-control rather than zero-loss assumptions are preserved in both languages.

prosePairReviews.scienceReason: A DC voltage equal to the allowed AC peak is explicitly an assumption of a simplified comparison, not an automatic insulation/corona equivalence. Comparable current limits and other constraints plus 'may' prevent a universal same-conductor power advantage. The steady-DC statement excludes AC inductive-reactance drop and continuing capacitive charging, not physical L/C, transient effects or conductor/corona/converter losses. No universal HVDC superiority or quantitative AC/DC ratio is asserted.
prosePairReviews.equivalenceReason: Both keep the same if-condition, comparable current/other constraints, possibility rather than guarantee, steady-state limitation, retained transient L/C effects and retained loss categories. The EN charging-current wording conveys the same ongoing AC capacitor charge/discharge effect as ZH.

prosePairReviews.scienceReason: The stated arrangement correctly puts AC voltage adjustment before rectification, inversion at the receiving end, and transformer adjustment on the resulting AC side. It is one arrangement, not a mandatory topology for all HVDC. Converter equipment/control/insulation and losses are acknowledged; an ordinary transformer is correctly denied direct steady-DC voltage conversion.
prosePairReviews.equivalenceReason: AC-to-DC rectifier and DC-to-AC inverter directions, equipment ordering, one-arrangement qualification, converter losses and the ordinary-transformer limitation agree exactly in concept.

prosePairReviews.scienceReason: Interconnection and coordinated generation/transmission can help manage demand peaks only when conditions permit. The text neither eliminates total demand peaks nor guarantees location-independent delivery; capacity, losses, operating state and faults remain constraints. The historical nationwide supply assertions are removed without unsupported modern replacement statistics.
prosePairReviews.equivalenceReason: Both describe the same interconnected power-system concept, conditional regional redistribution and morning/evening peak management. Both preserve the same denial of universal delivery/peak elimination and the same practical limits.
